opus-5.5.text:
Well, I wouldn't say it's a mistake to study it. The human hand is a marvel, and I have enormous respect for the people working on it. But I think it's a mistake to *start* there, to treat it as a prerequisite for useful manipulation.

The first issue is complexity. The human hand has something like 27 degrees of freedom, plus an extraordinary sensory system: thousands of mechanoreceptors in your fingertips, skin that deforms and conforms, tendons, all of it tightly integrated with a nervous system that's been refined over millions of years. When you try to replicate that mechanically, you end up with dozens of motors and cables and sensors packed into a very small space. Each one is a point of failure. These hands tend to be expensive, fragile, and very hard to control. Even when the hardware works, we don't have the control algorithms to take advantage of all those degrees of freedom. You've built a Stradivarius, and nobody knows how to play it.

The second point is that the parallel-jaw gripper, the simple two-finger pincher, and the suction cup are incredibly effective. If you look at the warehouses doing billions of picks, most of that work is done with suction cups and simple grippers. They're cheap, robust, and easy to model. My lab spent years on the Dex-Net project, and what we found is that if you pair a very simple gripper with good perception and good grasp planning, you can reliably pick up a huge variety of objects you've never seen before. The intelligence lives in the software, the perception and the planning, not in mimicking the anatomy.

There's a nice analogy with flight. Early inventors built machines with flapping wings because that's what birds did, and they mostly failed. The airplane worked by separating lift from propulsion, a fixed wing and a propeller. It didn't copy the bird; it understood the underlying principles. I think manipulation is similar. What matters is the physics of contact, friction, and uncertainty, not the five fingers.

And I'd add one more thing: humans themselves do a remarkable amount with very simple tools. Think of tongs, chopsticks, a surgeon's forceps. A surgeon with a pair of forceps can do extraordinarily delicate work. That tells you the bottleneck isn't the number of fingers. It's the perception, the feedback, and the judgment behind the tool.

So my view is: start simple, get reliable, deploy, collect data, and add complexity only when it's justified by the task. The humanoid hand might come eventually, but betting on it as the first step is, in my opinion, putting the cart before the horse.

r001.rationale: The response says a human hand has about 27 degrees of freedom and that such hands are very hard to control, making the connection between many joints and control difficulty clear.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention cable hysteresis or unreliable return to the same position when actuation reverses.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss hand weight reducing the payload a robotic hand can lift.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's a very natural instinct. We look at our own hands and we think, that's the gold standard, that's what evolution produced, so let's just copy it. And the human hand really is remarkable: 27 degrees of freedom, tendons, skin with incredible tactile sensing. But that's exactly the problem. When you try to build that, you end up with something that's enormously complex mechanically, very expensive, very fragile, and extremely hard to control. Every one of those joints needs an actuator, needs sensing, needs to be coordinated with all the others, and the failure modes multiply. I've seen a lot of these anthropomorphic hands in labs over the years, and many of them spend most of their time being repaired.

And the deeper issue is that we don't actually understand how humans use their hands. We have this intuition that we're doing something very sophisticated, and we are, but we can't articulate it. So copying the hardware doesn't give you the software, if you will. You've built the instrument but you don't know how to play it.

What I've found in my own work, and I think the field has largely found, is that you can get a surprisingly long way with much simpler grippers. A two-jaw parallel gripper, which is basically a pincer, or a suction cup. Those are what's actually working in warehouses right now. They're robust, they're cheap, they're easy to model, and they let you focus on the hard part, which is perception and planning: where do I put the gripper, how do I approach the object, what happens when I'm uncertain about its shape or its friction. Those are the questions that matter.

So my view is that the five-fingered hand is a bit of a distraction. It's a kind of romance with the human form, like the way early attempts at flight tried to flap wings like birds. The airplane doesn't flap. It turns out that once you understand the principles, you can often find a much simpler design that solves the actual problem. I'm not saying we'll never want dexterous hands, but I think starting there puts the cart before the horse.

r001.rationale: It says every joint must be coordinated with the others, making the hand extremely hard to control; this communicates the control difficulty caused by its many joints.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss cable-driven hands, hysteresis, or inconsistent return positions when actuation is reversed.

r003.rationale: It does not describe a tradeoff between the hand’s weight and the payload it can lift.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think it starts with confusing the goal with the mechanism. We want robots to do useful things in the world, but that doesn’t necessarily mean they should do them with the same anatomy we have.

A human hand is extraordinarily complex. You’ve got all these joints, tendons, and tactile sensors, and then a tremendous amount of brainpower devoted to controlling it. If you start by building a five-fingered hand, you’ve given yourself a very difficult control problem before you’ve even picked anything up.

For a lot of tasks, a simple two-finger gripper, or a suction cup, can be very effective. You can get a much more reliable system by choosing the mechanism to fit the task. That also lets you focus on the really interesting problems: figuring out where an object is, where to grasp it, and what to do when things don’t go as expected.

So I wouldn’t say five-fingered hands are never useful. But I think they’re a questionable starting point. Start with what you want the robot to accomplish, and add complexity when you have a reason to.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a five-fingered hand has many joints and creates a difficult control problem, clearly conveying the high-dimensional control challenge.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention cable-driven hands, hysteresis, or inconsistent return to position when actuation reverses.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss hand weight reducing the robot’s lifting payload.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it starts with the solution rather than the problem. We look at our hands, which are extraordinarily versatile, and assume a robot should have something similar. But a five-fingered hand introduces a huge amount of mechanical and control complexity before you’ve established what the robot actually needs to do.

If your task is to pick up a box, you may be able to do that with a suction cup or a simple two-finger gripper. Those are much easier to build, control, and make reliable. And reliability is a big deal: being able to do something once in a demonstration is very different from doing it thousands of times in a warehouse.

There are certainly tasks where a more dexterous hand would help. But I’d start with the task and ask what the simplest mechanism is that can accomplish it. The fact that we have five fingers doesn’t mean that’s the right starting point for a robot.
